utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for the witness -- we have read the report. Is there anything you want to add by way of direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What I have done, Your Honour, in one of the documents that is on its way, it's not really like the document with the former witness, I have created an outline of essentially -- some people would say "bullet points" about his report. And what I intended to do was, after explaining how he came to be involved in this project, the methodology employed in preparing his report, to put this list of bullet points on the ELMO and simply give him the opportunity to amplify the basis for his various conclusions without going through the report itself in any detail. So I would hope that we can do it -- my goal is to do it expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That may be a bit of a tall order, Your Honour, but I'll try very hard. Less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Scott, I think that the report is an historical report which goes far beyond the case that we are dealing with here, and as far as possible, one should avoid going into history in general. I don't think that would be very useful. But we should, rather, focus on the points related to the counts of the indictment --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) -- particularly regarding general facts. We all have the ability to study them ourselves. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The report itself is obviously heavily focused on -- not entirely but heavily focused on the events in Ahmici, but I understand the Court's guidance, and I apologise for the delay, Your Honour. Apparently we had some miscommunication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we start with the witness and the background matters? Is there any reason why we shouldn't start with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think we could, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: To save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can do that. Mr. McLeod? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, directing your attention to your background prior to becoming involved with the report that you did in 1993 concerning events in Central Bosnia, briefly by way of background, can you tell the Court, is it correct that you were a member of the British military, that is, the army, for approximately a ten-year period?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, what ranks did you hold?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: I joined as a private soldier, I was commissioned as a second lieutenant and promoted eventually to the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court some of the various tours of duty that you were involved in as they related to, in particular, postings to other foreign countries?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. I was initially posted to West Germany, as it then was; while I was there, I did a tour of West Belfast, which is not a foreign country but an interesting place; served in Belize and was also posted back into Northern Ireland for a two-year tour having completed my studies at university.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, as a result of your service up to the point of your -- was it your second tour then in Northern Ireland?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you awarded a medal or a ranking -- I'm not sure of the right word, and forgive me -- the honour of being a Member of the Order of the British Empire?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please use the other microphone because the interpreters cannot hear him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do we need to go back to anything? I'm sorry. If I can just ask the interpreters or ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no need to go back, but a pause between question and answer would be greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave the British army in approximately 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then become employed with something called the European Community Monitoring Mission?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I spent one year working for the ECMM employed by the British Foreign Office. I was doing two-month tours in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did six two-month tours for a total of one year?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure in this particular trial, Mr. McLeod, whether the ECMM has come up, or if it has, probably not very extensively, and it will come up more in the future, Your Honour. Can you tell the Court what was the ECMM and what the function was in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. The ECMM was established when the war in Yugoslavia first broke out in Slovenia. It was an international monitoring mission, initially just diplomats and then a mixture of diplomats and either serving or retired soldiers, and the basic pattern of operations was two-man teams with a driver and an interpreter would go and try and get a team on both sides of each of the confrontation lines, talk to the military and political leaders on both sides, and suggest initially that they should stop shooting at each other and then that they should try and establish various --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will you also please slow the witness down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What were the countries involved in its establishment?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: The basic countries were the European Community countries, and in addition, there were also a number of countries from what was then the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe, CSC, now the OSCE, so basically European countries plus Canada and Norway and Czechoslovakia, as it then was, and Poland. So quite a diverse mixture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you posted initially on joining, becoming involved with the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Initially I was working in Zagreb within Croatia working on both sides of the internal contact line between Croatian forces and Serb forces in Croatia. I was then based in the headquarters of ECMM in Zagreb in the humanitarian section. As a member of that group, I was involved in missions to northern Bosnia trying to re-establish a presence in northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could? It will ultimately make this quicker, I believe, if we now can distribute two documents, please? They are marked for identification purposes as Exhibits 2694.1 and 858.1. Your Honour, I think we can proceed. For the record, Your Honour, to guide the testimony, simply as an aid is what has been marked for identification as 2694.1. I do not intend to go back over the items we have already touched on which are discussed in the first several paragraphs of the first page, and I think we're down to the point where Mr. McLeod was appointed to the European Community Commission -- excuse me, European Community Monitoring Mission in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we can read the rest of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Exactly. That's why I prepared it. I thought it would be quicker than going through it in great detail by testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let us just read the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Shall I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Suffice it to say then, Mr. McLeod, that by the time you received an assignment as related to certain events in Central Bosnia in April 1993, you had been carrying out various functions and responsibilities in the former Yugoslavia for approximately nine months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not only with any particular ethnic group but virtually you had been involved, in fact, with essentially, at one time or another, all the ethnic groups; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then, please, now explain to the Court, how did you become to be assigned or involved in a mission, an ECMM mission, to Vitez in May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Certainly. After the events which had taken place in Vitez in April, a couple of things happened. The head of the regional centre in Zenica, a French ambassador, Jean-Pierre Thebault, came up to the headquarters to ask for resources for somebody to go down and help his humanitarian rep. to try and establish what had happened because everybody was very interested, and also a gentleman called Thomas Osorio, who is a human rights investigator, came to the ECMM at the same time and said that, quite clearly, the events that had taken place were of interest and it would be worth us as a group, the ECMM, trying to find out and establish impartially what had happened. So as these two events came together, it was suggested that I, as somebody who was in the humanitarian team in the headquarters, should be sent down to Zenica to work with the monitors already on the ground there to try and establish what had happened fairly rapidly and to write a report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And perhaps, for the record, it is a bit less cryptic, we've all been saying you were sent to Vitez because of "certain events" in April of 1993. Can you just -- what were those events, in a very short order, that caused the need for this mission to be recognised and carried out?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: There had been a period of tension between the Muslim and Croat sides in Central Bosnia, and this had appeared to erupt into violence in the Lasva Valley with a period of quite heavy fighting between the two parties, and in the aftermath of that fighting, it was clear that a number of things had happened, including the events at Ahmici, which is a village which appeared to be largely burnt. This was being quite heavily reported at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you, in fact, then go to the Vitez area in early May 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I travelled down on the 3rd of May, spent the next several days in the area, and travelled back up to Zagreb on the 12th and 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court whether -- when you went to Vitez on this mission, did you have any preconceived notions or tentative conclusions that you thought you would reach?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: It seemed -- it seemed quite clear that something had gone badly wrong. It was quite clear that there had been quite a lot of fighting going on. I was interested to try and talk to people on both sides of the confrontation at a number of different levels to ask them to tell me in their own words what had happened. As far as possible, I just wanted to get them to tell me what had happened so I could then draw some conclusions afterwards rather than accepting whatever the messages that seemed to be coming out of the media already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe, Mr. McLeod, that you approached this work with an open mind?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: That was certainly my intention, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before we get into the substance of your report, had you seen what came to be called and what we now refer to as "ethnic cleansing," had you seen events that were described or known to you as "ethnic cleansing" before going to Vitez in April -- excuse me, in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes. I had seen two separate sets of examples. I had seen the ethnic cleansing of Croats by the Serbs in the area of Croatia known as Krajina; that was those parts of Croatia that were controlled by Serbs. I had also seen ethnic cleansing of mostly Muslims but also Croats by the Serbs in northern Bosnia. So that the basic pattern was by then fairly familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, what are some of the indications or hallmarks of ethnic cleansing to you as a professional observer, a trained military man, and a professional observer? What would come -- when you see a village or a set of houses, what tells you that it may have involved ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I just object to this testimony on the ground that that calls for sort of an expert opinion, Your Honour, and this gentleman hasn't been identified as an expert, I don't think he is an expert. The requirements for expert testimony are very clearly outlined in the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence in Rule 94 bis, and they haven't been complied with here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that this is a helpful question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In due course, it can be dealt with. But, Mr. Sayers, there will come a time, no doubt, when this witness will be asked his opinion as a soldier, as a former soldier with ten years' experience behind him. Now, he is entitled to give that because of his training. But whether it's useful to go into these sort of things, I rather doubt. Can we move on, Mr. Scott? Could you bear in mind, please, not to go too quickly? I know you're trying to get through the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I apologise. I'm trying to do, I guess, many things at once, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Remember, we have this report and we've read the report, so the number of questions that we need in direct examination is limited. Bear in mind too that this witness has come to give his evidence, and it would be very inconvenient and a public expense if he has to come back to be cross-examined. Yes, let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention then to what's been marked as Exhibit 858.1, which has been previously distributed. For the Court and counsel, it is the two-column one-page chart, if you will. With that in front of you and recognising that the other parties -- the Court and other parties to these proceedings have a copy of this document, just tell briefly then what was the methodology or what did you do on arriving in the Vitez area in May of 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: The first thing that I did was talk to our own people on the ground and to UNPROFOR, particularly BritBat, to try and work out -- I gathered together all of the reports that had been written by UNPROFOR and ourselves, collated those, and tried to work out, from our reporting, what we thought had happened. Then I spoke to -- as you can see here -- a list of the people I met and talked to, a range of people on both sides, political, military, and religious, and asked them each to explain to me in their own words what they thought had happened leading up to the 16th of April and then immediately thereafter. On most occasions what I was trying to get them to do was to tell me what had happened and then to describe, with reference to a photocopied map so that they could identify various places on the ground, what had happened, and it was the basis of the conversations that I had had which I wrote down in my notebook which I then typed up and formed the basis of the report that I wrote.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at 858.1, can you just confirm that, in fact, you did each of these things, most of them are interviews but there are also some visits to particular locations, that you did all these things on or about the dates indicated in the right column?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, as indicated on the chart, in fact, visit Ahmici, the village of Ahmici, on the 4th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we would like to show a short video clip of an inspection of Ahmici at the time that Mr. McLeod was involved in that, which is marked as 1576. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. McLeod, in the interests of time, I didn't stop the clip, but there was a portion of a meeting that was -- a portion showing a meeting in the room, and you were shown in that clip; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were along on that inspection that day?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you, in fact, prepare a written report of your findings, which is obvious at this point, but for the record, did you do so?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown what's been marked as Exhibit 926, which I think virtually everyone has at this point in one form or another. While that's been done, Your Honour, I just observe, in response to Mr. Sayers, that this report, in fact, has been distributed and known to everyone, and the fact that Mr. McLeod was coming to testify has been known for a substantial period of time. So I think it's fair to say that no one is surprised about his report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit 926, Mr. McLeod, is that a copy or true copy of the report that you prepared, based on your work in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: This appears to be part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what other parts are there?

utterances.speaker: CHARLES McLEOD
utterances.text: Well, the copy that I've got goes as far as Appendix F, and I think it ought to go a bit further than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. Can you inspect what's been handed to you by the usher now, Mr. McLeod, and confirm if that's perhaps a fuller version that goes through Annex S?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the version that we've been provided only goes through Annex R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if the witness has got the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is the same as the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The same as the one you just -- all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a complete copy, Mr. Scott, --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm doing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- to give to the witness? Annex S, I see, is in fact the plan at the very back, if you've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The last page on my report is R15. It looks like it has a date stamp number of "02/02/66" on the bottom right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we have the same. The pre-last page is Annex F, which consists of one page and the text on the back, and enclosure to this annex which is marked as F3-3 on the bottom. That's the last one in the set.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously there has been a mistake, and if we can correct it, we will. If everyone wants to have the complete set, which I understand they do, then it will take moments to prepare that for everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us move on now, but make sure that Mr. Kovacic has a full copy by the time we adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, Mr. Nice reminds me, and I only raise it because given these technical problems, and I apologise, that it may be the better use of time -- I know there was discussion of other issues that were going to perhaps be raised today, and I know that Mr. Nice has some comments. Only because of these events, because of these problems, perhaps the better use of time, while these are being corrected, is to go to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, there shouldn't be these sort of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I fully agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And how long are you going to be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if we can get moving smoothly along, we can do it in another half hour to 35 minutes or so. It's a very important witness. I think even to do this witness in something less than an hour is really moving quite quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That may be, but we are adjourning, as you know, at lunchtime tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And there has to be cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Believe me, Your Honour, we've been aware of that all week long. We've been talking to Mr. McLeod about the scheduling issue, and unfortunately for -- well, mostly unfortunately for him, he understands that he may have to come back. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, half past 9.00 tomorrow. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What we have in mind is to sit at half past 9.00. Mr. Scott, if you would finish in half an hour, aim to do that, that will leave the Defence with three hours for cross-examination, which seems a generous portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To expedite matters, Your Honour, might I just ask if we could take a look at the contents of the materials that Mr. McLeod has brought with him just so we can inspect them overnight and maybe expedite the cross-examination tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there any difficulty about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If there aren't any different materials, no, there's no objection. His notes were -- personal notes were copied and provided to Defence counsel some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you might like to speak to the witness about it to see what else there is, and surely if there's no objection, to arrange that the Defence have a look at it overnight, which would speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we do that now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When I've said this: Mr. McLeod, could you be back tomorrow, please, at half past 9.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you remember, during the adjournment, apart from the matter which I've just mentioned, which is about your notes, not to speak to anybody about your evidence during the adjournment? But speak to Mr. Scott about your notes. I don't know what you've got, but perhaps you can explain it to him and, if necessary, it can be disclosed. If you have any objection to it being disclosed, then you must tell Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to go now, and we'll go on and deal with some procedural matters. (The witness withdrew) (Discussion off the record)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have quarter of an hour. We have to finish at 4.15 sharp. You had yesterday presented us with your proposed list of witnesses. We have now the Defence suggestions. They can't be anything more than that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think yesterday afternoon I was seeking to explain to the Court that what I had in mind, as revealed in my next list of witnesses, happens to accord very much with what you had indicated at the opening was provisionally in your mind, or minds, and I was noting that notwithstanding that congruence of our approach, that it's too early for an order to be made in this case, that there are important matters to be borne in mind, and that indeed this is a case where it's probably prudent to keep matters in mind generally and with both sides in view. Plainly, any limitation on the evidence I'm allowed to call is an important matter and one in which the Defence don't have a role. But I've dealt with that. A couple of realities, in light of the observations made yesterday and of which the Court must be careful. It is the defendant's actions over time and geography, charged, and their indictment confirmed by Judge McDonald and not severed, that makes this a large trial. A large trial does not have to be a long trial, and that's an important distinction that we've got to have in mind. What makes trials long, whether they are large or small in scope, is the number of matters that are genuinely in dispute. Now, I think one of the problems is that as we approach procedural issues, some of us here have the ability to talk in shorthand built on common experience, some of us don't, and it's easy to overlook that. It's easy perhaps not to appreciate exactly what's going on by way of the Defence approach to this case. The Court will, I think, now have appreciated that the Defence approach, certainly so far as Mr. Kordic is concerned and however elegantly expressed, is to restrict evidence wherever they can and to stop matters coming in. It is, if I may say so, a standard approach that has or had been used throughout common-law jurisdictions for centuries, and it can be very effective. But it's no longer acceptable, and it's got to be seen for what it is. When I deal with realities, I can deal in a sentence with this, the realities of common-law litigation, not that we're concerned with common-law litigation. We're concerned with, as Judge Robinson was wise to advise us of at an early stage, we're dealing with this jurisdiction, drawing on whatever is helpful from elsewhere, but otherwise following statute. But have in mind, just in the back of one's mind, a domestic murder in a common-law jurisdiction can involve from 50 or 100 witnesses and can be at its conclusion, with the jury directed, in between five or ten days, because when counsel on both sides are obliged to identify issues, a job that one judge once described, and I thought rather memorably, it was like filleting a fish, and he said that when he was directing a jury at lunchtime of the second day of a two-defendant trial of rape, and he said to the jury, "No Defence counsel is wrong when he said this has been a horrid trial." A day and a half provides a long time for a lot of material evidence, and so it does. But we can only use the human brain to half a lot of available evidence if counsel on both sides fillet the fish and present the Tribunal with what the Tribunal must have. Now, we, in this environment, cannot force the issue on the Defence, but the Chamber can. We have done everything we can to identify the case, to achieve agreement. We have offered to restrict ourselves in doing without evidence in chief, which is always better than a summary and always better than a, "Yes, I've read my statement, it's true." We saw that so convincingly very recently. We made all those offers. I can't think of any more that we can make, but we have done everything possible. The Defence on behalf of Mr. Kordic has admitted seven facts. They are facts about the independence of certain states and their recognition by the European Community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If the Defence say everything is in issue, whether that's a meritorious statement or not, but if they say that, suppose that to be the position, what do you suggest we do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if everything genuinely is in issue, then one of the consequences is that the trial will inevitably be longer than any of us might wish. Another consequence is that this Chamber, with its greater powers in relation to procedure than some domestic jurisdictions, will say, "Yes, everything may be in issue, but because of the conflicting interests facing us and mindful of our duty to all those interests and, of course, mindful of the standard of proof, we must nevertheless be prepared to accept evidence on a different basis." I'll give you a "for example", which is one I've raised in our overview of witnesses. The village witnesses. Now, we've been conditioned, by simply talking about the number of witnesses, to think somehow we've got to cut off the village witnesses. I've been conditioned to thinking that, as has the Chamber. I might have been far too willing to concede that, particularly in light of today's cross-examination on village witnesses who are identified as being hearsay. Maybe the argument is going to come in due course, "Well, you can disregard all that evidence because it's not first-hand." You'll remember the idea that I planned and for which I've been planning for a long time. As long ago as November of 1997, the statement of facts served on the Defence, supported by something like 100 village witnesses, identified an account, gave an account which you've seen in something called the Prosecutor's second invitation to admit. That document has been updated by a later approximately 40 or 50 witnesses and was a document I invited the Defence to admit. Mr. Kovacic, on behalf of Mr. Cerkez, did go some way towards making some qualified comments and admissions, and I'm grateful to him for his positive approach to the problems facing him. So far as Kordic is concerned, nothing. Now, the Tribunal might say that my proposal, that there should be an analyst let loose again -- it would be labour-intensive work but it would be worth doing, on all the available statements for the villages, to produce either that document or reproduce it or produce a different but similar version to it -- is an appropriate way of getting access to organised hearsay evidence. The witness could give evidence and the Defence could be obliged by the Chamber clearly to put what their positive case is in relation to those allegations, and then we could identify which and how many other live witnesses from the individual villages are required. But the very point that Your Honour raises has been in my mind as a matter of concern. Supposing it is said -- sorry. Start another way. Supposing I fall for the -- or we collectively yield to the blandishments that there must be only one or two witnesses per village and then the argument is it's not enough, supposing we yield to that and, at the end of the day, this Chamber has to write a judgement, can I respectfully invite the Chamber, when it is considering these matters, to look at that second invitation to treat as what you would be left with. I'll take simply a random page. So I'm on page 4. It's where it springs open. I've got a feeling it's the same village that sprang open in my opening, but it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not engaged]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, it came with the pre-trial brief of the Prosecutor. It's headed "The Prosecutor's Second Invitation to Admit Facts," and it looks like that. It's a tabulated document in that form. I had asked your offices to ensure it was available for you this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, I have it. Let's see how we get on. Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, and I can see the time. Incidentally, I promised that the last witness who I had to go and see, that in private session, if you grant me a private session, and in a minute I would speak on -- explain something to you, that will take a minute. So if we can close this part at 13 minutes past and go into private?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: At which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 4. I pick page 4 entirely at random, and I invite the -- it happens to be the village of Hercezi. I don't need to read it, but the question that I want the Tribunal to have in its mind is this: If and when it comes to -- well, it will write a judgement at some stage, one way or the other. We've been intimidated by speech of the number of witnesses to think that, for example, this village, but it will do for any, must be dealt with by one witness, with whatever limited -- or couple of witnesses, with whatever limited material that witness could provide and that that is all you'll be able to put into your judgements. As opposed to that, the Chamber may say to itself, "No, that can't be right. There is a great deal of material about this village, and when we make a judgement of this importance, present-day requirements and later historical judgements demand that we aren't put off by practical difficulties to doing with one witness saying whatever he can remember." The point is obvious. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that right? You see, you introduce the question of historical judgements, and I noticed you used that, Mr. Nice, in your last document that was put before us. We are concerned to try this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, do we need the amount of detail which appears in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would respectfully invite you to say you need much more something like that in some form or another than simply to proceed with one witness who may have come upon it after the event or who may have a partial view of the village or who can only see some of the events. It isn't as easy as all that to say it's going to be enough for any village simply to have one witness, in our submission to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, each time we talk about procedure, you are lecturing us. I think, after all, we have to see where we stand. We are at the Tribunal, you are in the Office of the Prosecutor, and we are trying to proceed in a practical manner. We don't need any lessons. We are in an International Tribunal. There is no complicity of any kind among the people here present. It is the will of the International Community that is at stake. I think there must be a total misunderstanding in what has been said so far. Nobody has said that we are going to pass a ruling which will close the doors to any future witnesses. We have said that we would like to have a rough idea of the necessary number of witnesses. It is up to you to say prima facie, at first sight, on the basis of an initial appreciation, and should you need, as you have just said, to develop your thesis further because the witnesses called were insufficient, you can apply for that, with argument, and then the Chamber will grant it. That is all that has been said so far. No one has said that the Chamber would authoritatively limit the evidence or the testimony that is going to be presented to this Tribunal, that has never been said, because our final objective is to establish the truth and we are all here in the service of the truth. You began well; you were on the right road, on the right track. You have told us about those above the line and below the line. You have made a categorisation. You know the case much better than anyone else for the moment. You can continue along that track. Try to concentrate on the essential witnesses for the moment, those who are willing and essential for the moment, under the reservation that, if necessary, you may make an additional appeal, the Chamber will examine it, and it may accept it, of course. We are not here innovating or revolutionising procedure. I think the objective set is to synthesise the witnesses as much as possible, which appears to be quite reasonable, because in no other case in this Tribunal have we had such a large number, and to have one witness a day with the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination included. I think that that seems to be quite reasonable and achievable. You have just said yourself that it is not normal for a trial to last two years. This has been criticised externally, and that is not normal. It is on that basis that our Chamber is working in cooperation with you, in the first place and, of course, we hope to have the cooperation of the Defence as well, and we are here to remind the Defence and you, yourself, each time, because that is our responsibility, as you know, and we are going to exercise that responsibility. I didn't wish to make a lecture but I ended up making one nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think, actually, Judge Bennouna and I are much more ad idem than he might think or I. If I can cut through it very quickly, my concern, as you will know from the list, is indeed at the moment to call above-the-line witnesses and indeed to take them ever more swiftly, by procedural devices that I have proposed and that I think, broadly speaking, will find favour with the Chamber. I am also concerned that the Chamber should do whatever it can to identify issues, as I can't do that, and that will enable us to go ever swifter. It will also enable me, I have no doubt, to cut down dramatically the number of witnesses every time that narrowing of issues is achieved. I see the time. I've got a number of other things I was going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll continue this, if there's time, tomorrow morning. That might be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. Can I say the one minute about the last witness in private session that I undertook to him I would?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Naumovski, if you wanted to say something about the debate as a whole, tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I was about to ask you if we may -- if we could have some 10, 20 minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we can get through the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ten or 20 minutes? I have a little trouble with that. Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4.19 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of May, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25
